About this document

This document provides the teaching content for Biology Years 12–13 of the
New Zealand Curriculum. Equivalent for Te Marautanga o Aotearoa is being
published separately.

Progress and assessment information for Biology Years 12–13 is still in development.
Once that is completed, Biology Years 12–13 is proposed to be made by the Minister
of Education as a National Curriculum Statement under section 90(1)(a) of the
Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Biology Years 12–13 will be required to start using it in Year 12 from
1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January 2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

  Students are taught about living systems focusing on how organisms function,
  interact, and evolve within biological systems. They use practical investigations to
  test and apply knowledge in areas such as cellular biology, genetics, ecological
  systems, body systems, and biotechnology.

Through the study of Biology, students draw on biological knowledge and practices
developed in earlier phases related to living systems, inheritance, and ecological
relationships. Learning builds from prior experiences to support students to explore
the interconnected nature of biological ideas across levels of organisation, from cells
and organisms to populations and ecosystems. Students strengthen their ability to
use biological knowledge, evidence, and models to explain patterns, processes, and
relationships within and between living systems.
Biology provides students with the knowledge and practices to analyse and apply,
evaluate and synthesise, represent and communicate disciplinary knowledge about
living systems. Through this disciplinary knowledge, students develop understanding
of how life functions, reproduces, responds, and changes over time, and how
biological explanations are constructed using evidence across molecular, organismal,
and ecological scales.
As students progress through Years 12–13, they are supported to develop
increasingly sophisticated abilities in data, systems, and situations using biological
concepts, models, representations, investigative methods, and where appropriate,
quantitative evidence.

  Biology leads to pathways in biology and related disciplines including biomedical
  science, environmental science, biotechnology, and health sciences.

Scientists communicate their ideas, evidence, and findings so they can be evaluated,
challenged, and used to inform decisions and actions.

Investigating in science

Scientists develop meaningful questions and use investigations to explain
phenomena. They gather or select evidence, collect primary data or source
secondary data, analyse data, identify patterns and relationships, evaluate evidence,
consider alternative explanations, and distinguish between strong and weak support
for claims. Scientists test theories by attempting to falsify them rather than prove
them.

In Years 12 and 13, students continue to investigate scientific questions, gather and
analyse evidence, and use this evidence to explain scientific phenomena and develop
their understanding of Biology.

Opportunities should be provided each year for students to undertake both practical
and secondary-source investigations, working independently and collaboratively.

Contexts and investigations may be selected or developed to reflect the needs and
interests of students, their community, and the local environment.

Delivery of Year 12 and 13 Biology programme must align with Safety and Science
guidance.

Further guidance on programme design, investigation opportunities, and resource
selection is available in the Biology Curriculum Support Document.

                         diseases, including inflammatory bowel disease and obesity
